description: Academic points mapped to teaching slides. Content is limited to the supplied pack and printed diagrams; image labels are preserved and masked selectively.

slides.title: Cell structure
teachingText: The nucleus, chromosomes, cell membrane, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes each have a function in the cell.
Let’s see how these structures control exchange, regulate cell activities, transfer energy and make proteins.

slides.title: Cells and organelles
teachingText: Cells are the basic units of living organisms.
Organelles are structures inside cells with specific functions. Together, they keep the cell functioning.

slides.title: Cell structure
teachingText: The cell membrane controls exchange. The nucleus and chromosomes are linked to proteins through genes. Mitochondria transfer energy into ATP, while ribosomes and ER are involved in protein production.
These links bring each structure together with its function.

slides.title: Cytoplasm
teachingText: The cytoplasm is jelly-like material outside the nucleus.
It contains organelles; the cell membrane forms the boundary around the whole cell.

slides.title: Cytoplasm
teachingText: The cytoplasm is the site of many chemical reactions, including anaerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration occurs in the cytoplasm. Most stages of aerobic respiration occur in mitochondria.

slides.title: Cell membrane
teachingText: The cell surface membrane is a partially permeable boundary.
It controls movement into and out of the cell.

slides.title: Cell membrane
teachingText: The cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell.
Substances cross the membrane by diffusion or through transport proteins.

slides.title: Cell membrane
teachingText: Substances cross the membrane by diffusion or through transport proteins.
These are ways of moving substances across the cell’s boundary.

slides.title: Cell membrane
teachingText: Active transport requires energy.
Substances cross the cell membrane by diffusion or through transport proteins.

slides.title: Cell membrane
teachingText: The cell surface membrane forms the boundary around the cell.
It is partially permeable and controls movement into and out of the cell.

slides.title: Nucleus
teachingText: The nucleus contains chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope separates it from the surrounding cytoplasm.

slides.title: Nucleus
teachingText: The nucleus controls cell activities by regulating protein synthesis.
The nucleus controls which enzymes are made and therefore which chemical reactions occur.

slides.title: Nucleus
teachingText: The nucleus controls which enzymes are made. It therefore controls which chemical reactions occur.
This is how regulation of protein synthesis controls cell activities.

slides.title: Nucleus
teachingText: A stained nucleus can often be recognised with a light microscope. It is often a prominent rounded or oval structure.
Appearance varies between cells and images. In a suitable TEM section, a nuclear envelope may be visible around it.

slides.title: Nuclear envelope
teachingText: The nuclear envelope separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm. It contains nuclear pores.
This boundary surrounds the nucleus. The cell membrane surrounds the whole cell.

slides.title: Nuclear pores
teachingText: Nuclear pores regulate passage of substances, including mRNA.
The pores are in the nuclear envelope, which separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm.

slides.title: Chromosomes
teachingText: Chromosomes consist of DNA associated with proteins.
They are contained in the nucleus and carry genes.

slides.title: Chromosomes
teachingText: Chromosomes carry genes that code for proteins.
The nucleus contains chromosomes, and chromosomes carry genes. This links the nucleus with protein synthesis.

slides.title: Chromosomes
teachingText: Chromosomes become condensed during cell division, making them easier to distinguish individually in suitable images.
They are not always visible as separate X-shaped structures.

slides.title: Chromosomes
teachingText: Chromosome organisation is covered under Genes, Chromosomes and DNA.
Here, chromosomes are DNA associated with proteins. They carry genes coding for proteins.

slides.title: Mitochondrion
teachingText: A mitochondrion has a double membrane.
Mitochondria are the site of most stages of aerobic respiration.

slides.title: Mitochondrion
teachingText: The mitochondrion is one of the structures inside a cell. It has a double membrane.
Its function is linked to aerobic respiration and energy transfer into ATP.

slides.title: Mitochondria
teachingText: Mitochondria are the site of most stages of aerobic respiration.
Energy released through respiration is transferred into ATP, which supplies energy for cellular work.

slides.title: Mitochondria
teachingText: Mitochondria transfer energy into ATP; they do not “make energy”.
Muscle cells and sperm cells contain many mitochondria to supply ATP for contraction or movement.

slides.title: Mitochondria
teachingText: Muscle cells and sperm cells contain many mitochondria.
These supply ATP for contraction or movement. A high demand for movement creates a high demand for ATP.

slides.title: Ribosomes
teachingText: Ribosomes may be free in the cytoplasm or attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum.
The ribosomes attached to rough ER join amino acids into polypeptides.

slides.title: Ribosomes
teachingText: Ribosomes are the site of translation. They join amino acids into polypeptides.
The ER processes and transports certain proteins. These are related roles in protein production.

slides.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
teachingText: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a membrane network of channels and flattened sacs.
The flattened membrane sacs are called cisternae.

slides.title: Rough ER
teachingText: Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, giving it its rough appearance.
In TEM, look for parallel membrane profiles with small dark particles attached. The attached particles are ribosomes.

slides.title: Rough ER
teachingText: Rough ER helps fold and process proteins made by its attached ribosomes.
These proteins may be destined for secretion or cell membranes. Ribosomes build the polypeptides; the ER processes certain proteins.

slides.title: Rough ER
teachingText: Rough ER supports transport of certain proteins in vesicles.
Assembly, processing and transport are related steps, with different structures responsible for each role.

slides.title: Smooth ER
teachingText: Smooth ER has no ribosomes attached.
Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface. This gives the two forms of ER their different appearance.

slides.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
teachingText: The key visible distinction is the presence or absence of attached ribosomes.

slides.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
teachingText: The ER is connected to the nuclear envelope.
The nuclear envelope separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm; the ER is a membrane network of channels and flattened sacs.

slides.title: Smooth ER
teachingText: Smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification and Ca²⁺ storage.
It has no ribosomes attached.

slides.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
teachingText: ER is a site of protein and lipid synthesis. Rough ER is involved in protein synthesis, modification and transport.
Ribosomes join amino acids into polypeptides. ER processes and transports certain proteins.

slides.title: Cytoplasm
teachingText: Amino acids attach to tRNA in the cytoplasm, not specifically in ER.
Ribosomes join amino acids into polypeptides. ER processes and transports certain proteins.

slides.title: Ribosomes and ER
teachingText: Individual ribosomes and ER membranes are not resolved by an ordinary light microscope.
In suitable TEM images, ribosomes may appear as small dark particles, free in the cytoplasm or attached to rough ER.

slides.title: Light microscopy
teachingText: A stained nucleus can often be recognised with a light microscope. Condensed chromosomes may be visible in suitable dividing cells.
Individual ribosomes, transport proteins and fine ER membrane details require greater resolution.

slides.title: TEM
teachingText: TEM images show thin sections and can reveal internal cell structures. The same kind of organelle can look different when cut in different orientations.
Membrane boundaries, membrane networks and small particles provide clues to the structures.

slides.title: Microscope recognition
teachingText: A dark patch alone does not prove a structure is a nucleus. An oval shape alone does not prove it is a mitochondrion.
Visible structure and context support an identification. Clearer features make a structure easier to recognise.

slides.title: Microscope recognition
teachingText: The diagrams in this lesson are schematics.
The checkpoints cover structure names, recognition knowledge and functions. Real-micrograph identification is not assessed here.

slides.title: Cell structure
teachingText: The six structures are linked with their functions below. A final set of questions brings these relationships together.
